The walls in this building are so thin I can hear my neighbor's alarm clock through them, and yet you charge premium rent like this is some kind of luxury accommodation. The hallway light has been broken since January. The elevator is a death trap. The intercom dials a wrong number. You have collected hundreds of thousands of dollars from this building and reinvested approximately nothing back into the maintenance of it. Slumlord behavior with a designer aesthetic.

Three months later they quietly removed the apology from their website. The page redirects to a feel-good corporate values landing page. The harm is unaddressed. The promised reforms were never implemented. The task force never met. The community is still waiting. And the executives who issued the apology are now at different companies, doing the same things, getting ready to apologize for them too.

Parking enforcement gave me a ticket while I was inside the post office returning a misdelivered package on behalf of the city. Inside the city's own building. For a meter that had expired by ninety seconds. The audacity of an institution that cannot manage its own mail somehow finding the bandwidth to ticket a citizen for a minor delay is breathtaking. I am contesting it. I am winning. I am demanding an apology in writing.

The operating system updated itself overnight without permission, restarted my computer in the middle of an unsaved document, and now it is downloading additional updates that it claims are mandatory. I did not consent. I was not asked. The work I lost was hours of irreplaceable effort. The new interface is worse. The buttons have moved. The icons are different colors for no reason. Every update from this company is a step down from the previous version and a step toward my early grave.

Why does opening a single document require accepting six dialogues, dismissing three popups, signing into two accounts, and waiting ninety seconds for the splash screen to finish congratulating itself? My document is forty kilobytes. My laptop has thirty-two gigabytes of RAM. There is no excuse for this. None. Software engineers used to make programs that worked. Now they make ad delivery platforms with a side feature of occasionally opening files.

Do not lecture me about the importance of your product when I have told you four times that I am not interested. I do not need to hear about the limited time offer. I do not need to hear about how this will save my family money. I do not need to hear another word from you. The audacity of arguing with someone in their own home, over a phone line they pay for, about a product they have already declined, is breathtaking.

The DMV has somehow gotten worse. I did not think it was possible. I was wrong. There is now an online appointment system that crashes every time you try to book an appointment, and an in-person walk-in line that the staff actively pretends not to see. The clerks rotate every fifteen minutes so that no one has to deal with the same angry citizen twice. Whoever ran this place into the ground deserves a special wing of municipal hell.

The website tells me I need to bring three forms of identification. I bring three forms of identification. The clerk tells me one of them does not count. I ask which one would have counted. He says he cannot tell me, that depends on the situation. There is no situation. There is only the situation of me standing here, with my paperwork, trying to do the thing the website told me to do. The contempt for citizens is total.

The form to request reimbursement for an interrupted trip is seventeen pages long, requires receipts I cannot get at midnight in a strange city, and has a sixty-day processing window. Sixty days. To get back money you took from me weeks ago for a service you failed to deliver. The asymmetry between your speed of charging and your speed of refunding is the entire grift, and I am going to talk about it loudly and publicly until my refund clears.

Listen up. This company has stolen money from at least six people I personally know, including me. They take your deposit, they string you along with vague promises about timelines, and then they disappear when it comes time to deliver. I have receipts. I have screenshots. I have testimonials from former employees who left because they could not stomach being part of the scam. Do not give them a dollar. Do not give them your phone number. Do not give them the time of day.

The way you started your reply with um, actually tells me everything I need to know about how this conversation is going to go. You are not correcting me. You are performing correction for the benefit of whoever is watching, in the hope that you might score a point. There is no point. There is no audience. There is just a bunch of strangers who have collectively decided you are exhausting and your contributions are not worth engaging with.

The mechanic looked me dead in the eye and quoted nine hundred and forty dollars for a brake job that another shop is doing for two-fifty. He cited proprietary parts, certified technicians, and shop diagnostics, none of which mean anything in a context where the part is twenty bucks on the internet. He thought I would not check. He thought I was too embarrassed to question him. He thought wrong.

Cancel button is buried six menus deep, behind a survey, behind a retention offer, behind a confirmation page, behind a please reconsider screen, behind a final warning, and finally, behind a chat window with a human whose entire job is to make me regret leaving. I have not regretted leaving anything more in my life than I regret signing up for this in the first place. The signup took eleven seconds. Cancellation has now taken forty-five minutes.

I have lived through three lane reductions, two bridge closures, one phantom construction project that lasted four years, and now they are tearing up the same stretch of road they finished six months ago. Who is in charge of this? Are they actively trying to make commuters miserable? The answer must be yes, because there is no other rational explanation for the sustained assault on basic mobility this city has waged against its own residents.

The website crashed during the final submission and the form has to be filled out again from the beginning, on a different browser, between the hours of four and six in the morning when fewer users are online. This is the official advice from the department. Wake up at four in the morning to submit your tax extension. The IT department has surrendered. The agency has surrendered. The state has surrendered. The citizens are still expected to perform.

The website overlays a fifteen-second unskippable video before allowing me to read a single sentence. Then it overlays another one between paragraphs three and four. Then it overlays a third before the conclusion. By the end of the article I have watched more advertising than journalism. The actual article is competent, but the experience of consuming it has been actively hostile to my time and attention, and I will not be back.

Telling a paying customer that their refund request will be processed in six to eight weeks is corporate cowardice. You took my money in two seconds, but returning it takes two months? Pure contempt for customers, dressed up in policy language. I want a human to look me in the digital eye and explain why a multi-billion-dollar company cannot process a refund as quickly as it processes a charge. The double standard is infuriating.

The food delivery app advertised free delivery on this order. The total at checkout includes a service fee, a small order fee, a busy area fee, a driver tip suggestion that defaults to twenty-five percent, and a regulatory response fee that I am pretty sure is not regulatory. The free delivery cost thirteen dollars in fees. The food, which was twelve dollars at the restaurant, arrived for thirty-one dollars total. The app is laundering markups through opaque accounting.

Forty minutes I waited on the phone for a representative to tell me that my issue was not in their department and I should call a different number, which I had already called, which transferred me back to this one. The cycle continues. The cycle is the point. The cycle is designed to make me hang up so they can avoid actually solving anything. Well I am not hanging up. I have all day. I have a backlog of grievances and I am ready to deliver them.

Whoever decided that every movie now needs a connected universe should be exiled from Hollywood. I do not want to watch eleven hours of setup for a payoff that is itself just setup for the next eleven hours. I want a story. With a beginning. And a middle. And an end. Not a franchise. Not a content delivery vehicle. A film. Like we used to make. Like adults used to enjoy.

He has installed monitoring software on my laptop. It tracks keystrokes, mouse movements, and screen activity. It reports periods of inactivity to his dashboard in real time. I am being surveilled to verify that I am working. I am a senior professional with a decade of experience and he is timing my bathroom breaks. The dignity has not just left the room. The dignity has been chased out with a stick.

The coworker who has been at the company for three months is now explaining the project to me. To me. The person who built it. He has read the documentation, which I wrote, and has helpful corrections about how I have structured the work. He is delivering these corrections as advice, in a friendly tone, as if I will be grateful. I am not grateful. I am furious that I have to smile and nod while he repackages my own ideas back to me as wisdom.

Your bag fees are extortion, your seats are torture devices, your in-flight food is an insult, and your customer service is a black hole into which all reasonable requests disappear forever. I have flown on military transports with better hospitality. I have ridden Greyhound buses with more legroom. The next time I voluntarily board one of your planes, it will be because every other airline on earth has gone out of business and I have no other choice.

Stop charging me thirty-five dollars for a salad. It is lettuce. The lettuce is not magic. The lettuce did not cure cancer. The lettuce is not the answer to climate change. It is a leaf and some dressing in a paper bowl, and the only thing extraordinary about it is the markup. The whole industry of bourgeois health food is feeding nothing except the bank accounts of the people running it.

The bank charges a monthly maintenance fee for an account I have had for fifteen years, which was originally fee-free. The fee was introduced silently three years ago and has been climbing ever since. The notification of the fee change was buried in a quarterly mailer that looked like junk and was almost certainly thrown away. The bank knows. The bank counts on this. The whole institution is engineered to extract small amounts from inattentive customers in volume.

The adjuster came to look at the storm damage, spent ten minutes glancing at the roof from the ground, and submitted a report that the damage was preexisting and not covered. The damage was not preexisting. We have photographs from before the storm. We have neighbors who watched it happen. The denial is a fabrication, and the appeals process is designed to outlast the patience of homeowners trying to repair their lives. Disgraceful.

The ad blocker blocked the ad. The site detected the ad blocker. The site posted a snarky note telling me to disable the ad blocker. I disabled the ad blocker. The site loaded forty-seven autoplay videos and crashed my browser. I re-enabled the ad blocker. The site refused to load until I turned it off. I have closed the tab. I have closed the site. I will never return. There are other places that talk about the news.

The compensation policy states that delays caused by air traffic control are not eligible for refunds. The delay was caused by the airline overbooking the flight and waiting for volunteers to give up their seats. The airline has classified this as an air traffic control delay in its records. The classification is a fiction. The fiction is corporate self-preservation. The customer service team will not respond to the discrepancy and the dispute process requires fifty pages of documentation.

The update removed three features I used daily and added four features I did not ask for. The features that were removed had clear utility. The features that were added are clearly designed to push me toward the paid tier or to monetize my data in some way I cannot articulate but can sense in my bones. The product is worse. The product is always worse after an update. The pattern is so reliable I should be charging consulting fees.

The terms of service for this update are eighty-two pages long, half of which exist solely to indemnify the company against the harms its own software causes. I have to agree before I can read my own emails. This is not a contract. It is a hostage note. And the option to disagree closes the program, locks me out of my account, and deletes my data. Pure corporate intimidation, dressed up in pop-up form.

The political mailer is a glossy oversized postcard featuring an unflattering photograph of a candidate I have never heard of, accusing them of crimes that did not occur, in a font that is hard to read by design. The bottom of the card lists the funding source as a PAC with a vaguely patriotic name that nobody has ever investigated. I will throw this away. I will throw away eleven more like it. The forests cleared for this nonsense will haunt our descendants.

Stop showing me ads for things I literally just bought. The whole point of the data harvesting was supposedly that the targeting would be useful. It is not useful. It is haunting. I bought one pair of shoes and now every platform on the internet shows me variations of those shoes for the next four months. Either build a better algorithm or stop pretending the surveillance has any benefit to the user. It does not.

The pickup truck that tailgated me for six miles this morning had a bumper sticker about respecting the troops. I would like to inform him that nothing about driving four inches behind another car at seventy miles an hour respects anyone, least of all the people who fought so he could be alive to be this stupid. Back off. Just back off. You are not impressing anyone with your aggressive driving except other morons.

The verification system that used to mean something has been sold to anyone with seven dollars and zero standards. Now I cannot tell the difference between actual news organizations and impersonator accounts. Now scams are easier than ever to run because anyone can buy the same badge of legitimacy. The platform has eaten its own credibility for a small monthly subscription fee, and the consequences are spilling out into the real world.

The status update says the address was not accessible. The address has been accessible to every other delivery driver who has visited it in fifteen years. The address is on a paved street with clear signage and a numbered mailbox. The driver simply did not feel like making the stop. He marked it inaccessible and moved on. The carrier will defend this judgment for as long as it takes me to give up.

The session timed out. The form is gone. The data I entered, over the course of forty-three minutes, painstakingly, with documents pulled from filing cabinets across the house, is gone. The timeout warning gave me ten seconds to respond, hidden in a popup behind the main window where I could not see it. The form must be re-completed in full. There is no draft mode. There is no save. The platform was designed by people who hate human beings.

Sixteen hours. Sixteen hours I have been sitting in this terminal because your gate agents have given me three different stories about what is happening with my rebooking. The first one said tomorrow morning. The second said the day after. The third said she did not know and I should check the app. The app says the flight has been canceled. The flight that was supposed to replace the canceled flight has now been canceled. I have lost my mind.

I am genuinely furious that anyone gave this place a star, a recommendation, a passing thought. The risotto was glue. The salad had a bug in it. The bug had more personality than the entire waitstaff combined. When I complained, the manager shrugged and said that's how it comes, as if culinary mediocrity were a fixed law of physics. I want my money back and an apology in writing.

Spare me the gotcha. You did not catch me in anything. You misread my post, replied to a strawman of your own creation, and then declared victory before anyone else had even seen it. This is not how arguments work. This is performance. You are arguing with a fictional opponent who agrees with you that I am wrong. The rest of us are over here, watching you flail at a ghost, and it is genuinely sad to watch.

Six guys are sitting on the bench press taking turns at a leisurely pace and chatting about supplements between sets. They are using the bench. They are not using the bench. They are leaning against it. They are scrolling on their phones near it. They have effectively claimed the bench as their hangout zone. The rest of us, who came here to actually work out, are waiting at a polite distance, growing visibly more annoyed, while they remain oblivious or pretend to be.

The gym contract listed the monthly fee in big bold print and the annual maintenance fee in tiny print at the bottom of page three, where I did not read it. The annual maintenance fee is sixty dollars and arrived as a surprise charge in March. The cancellation requires sixty days' notice in writing, certified mail, to a specific address that is not on the website. The cancellation will not be honored if it does not include the original membership card, which I lost five years ago. The contract is a labyrinth and the gym is the minotaur.

The save button is at the top of the form. The submit button is at the bottom of the form. The form does not save automatically. If you forget to save before clicking submit, the form fails validation, takes you back to the top, and discards everything below your save point. I have lost an hour of work to this design choice. The developer responsible has, I assume, never used a form in their life.

I have been in meetings since nine in the morning. I have not done any actual work today. I will not do any actual work today. I will go home, sleep poorly, and return tomorrow to a calendar full of more meetings, during which I will be asked why I am behind on the deliverables I cannot possibly deliver because I am perpetually trapped in this purgatory of speakerphones and slide decks.

Your IVR system asked me to describe my problem and when I said the word refund it transferred me to the sales department, where a human being who was clearly already exhausted asked me to start over from the beginning. I have started over from the beginning four times. The next person who tells me to hold while they transfer me is getting a complaint filed against them personally. I am keeping a list. With names.

An entire family has formed at the register, with cousins arriving one by one, each handing the cashier a new item or coupon, while the matriarch consults a hand-written list and the patriarch insists on returning one specific brand of bread that they have already decided against three times. The line is no longer a line. It is a slow national tragedy, unfolding in real time, with us as both witnesses and victims.

Every email reply takes seventy-two hours, every reply asks me a question I already answered in the original email, and every escalation sends me back to the start of the queue. The system is designed to wear me down until I give up and stop bothering you. I see what you are doing. I am not giving up. I will keep emailing every seventy-two hours for the rest of my natural life if I have to.

The motorcycle club has decided that the loop outside my window is their preferred riding route. They come through in groups of twenty, engines modified for maximum volume, late at night, weekly. The route is a public street. The volume is technically within limits because the limits were written before this particular class of exhaust system was invented. The law is from a quieter era. The enforcement is from a fictional one.

The doorbell camera caught the driver kicking my package into the bushes because it would not balance on the railing. He then took a photo, presumably of the bush, and called it delivered. I had to crawl through the hedge in business clothes to retrieve my own package. The shrubbery has scratched the box. The contents have shifted. I will be filing a complaint, a chargeback, and an unkind review with a still frame from the doorbell as the cover image.

The game app, an actual children's game, has requested microphone access. To play the game. The microphone is not used in the game. There is no voice interaction. There is no recording feature. The microphone permission is a data acquisition mechanism for the parent company's broader analytics platform. The app is a Trojan horse and the children using it are the targets. The fact that this is legal is one of the great moral failures of the modern app ecosystem.

I do not understand the awards. I do not understand the laudatory reviews. I do not understand the book club discussions that have somehow turned this thin, joyless novel into a generational touchstone. The characters are flat. The dialogue is wooden. The themes are so heavily underlined that I expected highlighter on the page. There is no there there. The emperor is naked and the critics are too embarrassed to mention it.

The scam call that pretended to be my elderly mother's pharmacy nearly tricked her into giving up her Medicare number. Nearly. Because I happened to walk in and hear what she was saying. The people who run these operations target the most vulnerable, the most isolated, the most trusting, and they sleep fine at night. Whatever circle of hell exists for those who prey on the elderly, I hope each of them has a reserved seat.

A new recurring meeting has been added to my calendar without my knowledge or consent. It is called sync-up and it has no agenda. It meets every other Wednesday for ninety minutes. No one knows who scheduled it. No one knows what it is for. Everyone attends out of fear that not attending would be perceived as not engaging. We are all hostages of a recurring calendar invite that no one has the authority to cancel.

The office is open from nine to four, closed for lunch from twelve to one-thirty, closed on the second Tuesday of every month for staff training, closed on every federal and state holiday, and apparently closed at random intervals for reasons no one will explain to me. I have taken three days off work in the last month to come here, and each time I have arrived to find the doors locked and a sign apologizing for the inconvenience. This is not government. This is theater.

The concert venue charged me twenty-two dollars for a beer in a plastic cup, served by a teenager who could not have cared less. Twenty-two dollars. For a beer. The brewery that made it sells it for three. The markup is eight hundred percent and the venue justifies it by saying the costs of doing business have risen. The costs have risen. They have risen because they keep raising them. The circular reasoning is breathtaking.

The discourse around this album is genuinely embarrassing. Critics are tripping over themselves to declare it a masterpiece because the artist is famous, but the songs are derivative, the production is bloated, and the lyrics read like a tenth-grade journal. The emperor has no clothes, and the entire music press is enthusiastically describing the cut of his invisible jacket. Have some standards. The audience certainly does, even if you do not.

Three weeks. Three weeks I have been without hot water, and your maintenance guy has shown up exactly once, declared he needed a part, and vanished into the ether. I am paying full rent for a unit that does not have functioning plumbing. I am bathing at the gym. I am washing dishes in the sink with water boiled in an electric kettle. The next email I send is going through the housing court, and you can explain yourself to a judge.

The referee ejected my favorite player for arguing a call, even though the player was being respectful and the call was, demonstrably and on multiple replays, wrong. The thin-skinned officiating culture in this league has become a parody. You cannot question a bad decision without being kicked out. You cannot show emotion without being penalized. The entire system protects the people in stripes from accountability, and the rest of us pay the price.

I just got disconnected after eighty-three minutes on hold and the callback feature lied to my face about preserving my place in the queue. The automated voice cheerfully informed me to please try again later as if it had not just stolen an hour and a half of my afternoon. Try again later. I will try again later. With a lawyer.

The clerk read my driver's license number out loud in a busy lobby and then asked me to confirm my social security number at full volume. There is no privacy. There is no security. There is no concern. The clerk has been doing this for years and no one has stopped her, and the people in line can now apply for credit cards in my name if they have a working memory. I am beyond complaint. I am into despair.

My internet has gone down four times this week and your outage map keeps showing all green in my area. Either the map is broken or your customer service is gaslighting me. I have video of the modem flashing red. I have screenshots of the speed test reading zero. The denial of an obvious problem is not customer service, it is corporate cowardice, and I am tired of having to prove that the service I pay for is not working.

Calling everyone who disagrees with you a shill is not an argument. It is the last refuge of someone who has lost the argument and refuses to admit it. We are not paid by anyone. We just happen to know things about a topic you clearly do not. Disagreement is not a conspiracy. It is the natural consequence of being incorrect in a public space. Grow up. Learn. Or leave.

Do not tell me it is the weather. There is no weather. The sun is shining. The planes are taking off. The plane I was supposed to be on left twenty minutes ago, empty, because you decided cancelling the flight was cheaper than waiting for the gate-checked bags to be returned. The whole industry has decided that lying to passengers about weather is easier than admitting their crew-scheduling is a mess. We see through it. We always have.

Park in your own driveway. There is plenty of room. There is so much room. And yet for some reason your son chooses to park his oversized truck directly in front of my mailbox every single day, blocking my access and forcing the mailman to skip me half the time. I have asked nicely. I have asked less nicely. The next conversation is going to be with the city about parking enforcement, and I hope his truck gets towed all the way to the next county.

Every female character in this novel is described first by her body and second by her hair, with personality coming a distant third if it comes at all. The author is a grown man writing in twenty-twenty-five and apparently has not noticed that the world has moved on. The dialogue is unbearable. The romance is implausible. The whole book reads like a fever dream from a writer who has been talking to no one but his agent for fifteen years.

The official apology was followed within hours by an internal memo, leaked to the press, instructing all employees not to use the word sorry in any communication with customers. The official position is contrition. The actual position is litigation defense. The disconnect between what they say outside the building and what they say inside it tells you everything you need to know about how seriously they take any of this.

The personal trainer has commandeered three machines and the entire stretching area for one client. Three. For one client. The rest of the gym is squeezed into the remaining floor space while a single paying customer enjoys a private studio experience at our expense. The trainer is not even working with the client most of the time. He is on his phone. The client is texting. The machines sit idle while the rest of us circle like vultures.

I would rather have a tooth pulled without anesthesia than spend one more second listening to your menu options have recently changed please listen carefully. They have not changed. They have never changed. They will never change. The menu is the same wretched gauntlet it was the last forty-seven times I called and your suggestion that I listen carefully is an insult to my intelligence and my time.

The ad has now been retargeted across every site I visit because I once clicked on a pair of shoes at midnight in a moment of weakness. The shoes follow me. They are on the news site. They are on the recipe site. They are on the page about Roman history. The same pair of shoes, animated, dancing, suggesting in increasingly aggressive terms that I should reconsider. I have reconsidered. The reconsidered position is that I will never buy those shoes, and I will boycott the brand.

The barking dog has barked continuously for three hours. The owner is not home. The owner has not been home for hours. The owner leaves the dog outside for the entire workday. The animal services line is unstaffed after hours. The non-emergency police line transferred me to animal services. The HOA secretary told me to leave a note on the door. I have left twenty notes. The notes are part of the landscape now. They are weathered and unread.

Every single update makes the app worse. The button I used daily has been moved. The button I never use has been promoted to the front. The dark mode now looks like dirty pond water. The font has changed for no reason. The new logo is offensive to my eyes. Whoever is in charge of UX at this company should be relieved of duty, and the previous version of the app should be restored by court order if necessary.

I do not understand the praise. I do not understand the awards. I do not understand the standing ovations at festivals. The emperor is naked and apparently I am the only one willing to say so. This film is a meandering, self-important slog dressed up in beautiful cinematography and mistaken for depth. There is nothing here. The themes are obvious. The acting is mannered. The ending is a shrug. Pure cinematic vanity.

The article cuts off after the first sentence with a wall of subscription options that requires me to either commit to ten dollars a month or close the tab. There is no option to read this single article. There is no option to pay a quarter for the piece. There is only the all-or-nothing wall, designed by someone who fundamentally misunderstands the rhythms of casual reading. I am closing the tab. I am not subscribing. The publisher gets neither my money nor my attention.

You changed the policy on dogs without notifying any tenants. People who signed leases with their pets are now being told they have thirty days to find new homes for them. Are you out of your mind? You cannot unilaterally rewrite a lease. This is going to court. It is going to a journalist. It is going to every review site that will host the screenshots. You have miscalculated, and you are about to find out.

The agent kept reading from a script even when I had already addressed every point on it. I do not need to be told my call is important to you. If it were important to you, I would not have spent the better part of a Saturday afternoon shouting at an automated menu system. Words mean things. Stop using nice ones to paper over the cruel reality of what this experience actually is.

The stranger on the train has just informed me that my book is overrated, that the author is problematic, and that I should be reading something else entirely. He did not ask what I think of the book. He did not introduce himself. He simply opened the conversation with a critique of my reading material as if I had requested a review. I am putting on headphones. I am turning to the window. I am, for the rest of this train ride, a wall.

The villain in this movie spends the entire runtime explaining his master plan, which turns out to make absolutely no sense when subjected to any logical scrutiny. Why kidnap the scientist if you already have the formula? Why blow up the dam if your goal is to flood the city you live in? The screenwriters did not think this through. The director did not care. And the producers banked on the audience being too distracted by explosions to notice.

Saturday morning at the gym has become a public-square performance of who can be the most inconsiderate. People are doing supersets across half the floor. People are filming themselves in front of the equipment. People are wandering aimlessly between machines, holding them with their hand for no reason, occupying space without using it. The gym has more than enough equipment if everyone used it efficiently. The gym is unusable because no one does.

The number I called from the website is no longer in service. The replacement number on the new website is for a different department. The voicemail at the correct department is full. The email address I finally found leads to an automated reply telling me to call the original number. I am running in concentric circles. I have aged visibly. My family has lost track of me. Whoever designed this system should be tried for crimes against time.

Every package delivery text that asks for a payment to release my package is a scam. Every email from the IRS demanding action is a scam. Every social media DM from someone claiming to be tech support is a scam. I have stopped trusting anything unsolicited, and I am furious that this is the world we live in. The criminals have ruined every normal channel of communication, and we accept it because we have collectively given up.

You canceled my flight without notifying me. I drove to the airport. I parked the car. I checked my bag. I went through security. I sat at the gate. The gate agent looked at me with confusion and said the flight had been canceled six hours earlier. Six. Hours. Earlier. Your notification system has one job and it failed at the most basic level. I am furious. I am exhausted. I am demanding a refund and parking reimbursement in writing.

The app updated and reset its permissions. The location permission, which I had carefully denied, is now on. The microphone permission, which I had explicitly revoked, is now on. The app is now monitoring me again, and the only way to find out was to manually inspect each permission, which the OS does not surface clearly. The trust I had developed with the operating system has eroded. The trust I had developed with the app never existed.

Every supporting character exists solely as a sounding board for the protagonist's anguished introspection. They have no inner lives, no motivations, no purpose beyond reflecting the central figure's brilliance back at him. The novel is essentially a solipsistic monologue with occasional human furniture. By the end I wanted to write apology letters to the imaginary friends who were forced to share pages with this insufferable man. Tedious. Self-important. Forgettable.

Stop telling me my issue has been escalated. It has not been escalated. It has been moved from one queue to another queue where it will sit for another two weeks before someone with the same lack of authority looks at it and moves it again. The word escalated has lost all meaning. It now means abandoned. Just say abandoned. At least be honest about it.

Three deliveries this week tossed across the porch from the curb. Not placed. Not laid down. Tossed. One of them is a crate marked fragile, glass, this side up. The driver hurled it underhand and drove off before it stopped sliding. The contents are obviously broken. The carrier will demand photographs and a thirty-day investigation. By the time anyone reviews it, the company will have decided that the packaging was insufficient and refused the claim.

If you cannot figure out how a four-way stop works after thirty years of having a license, you should not be on the road. You should be on a tricycle in your driveway, supervised. The guy in the white sedan today sat at the intersection for a full ten seconds with no one else around, then floored it through the stop sign as I was already halfway through. I hope his insurance premiums quadruple overnight.

The author's previous novels were sharp, funny, and economical. This one reads like he fired his editor, his agent, and possibly his entire reading group, and decided to publish his first draft as a statement of artistic freedom. The statement received. The artistic freedom is noted. The book is a mess. Go back to the editor. Go back to the structure. Go back to the discipline that made you worth reading in the first place.

He wants to be looped in on every decision. Every decision. The decision about which font I just complained about. The decision about which calendar invite color to use. The decision about who orders lunch when the team is in the office. I am no longer empowered to make any decision at all. I have outsourced my judgment to a man whose own judgment is comically poor, and the work product is suffering accordingly.

Your supervisor is not going to defend you. Your supervisor knows the script you are reading from is bordering on fraud. Your supervisor is just hoping you hit your quota before someone reports the whole operation. Find a different employer. Find one whose customers do not hang up on you with rage in their voices. This is not a career. This is a slow erosion of your soul one phone call at a time.

The film opens with a voiceover so condescending it might as well be a public service announcement, then proceeds to spend the next two hours explaining its own themes in case the audience is too stupid to keep up. We are not too stupid. We are insulted. Treat us like adults or do not invite us to the theater. The director's contempt for his own audience radiates off the screen in waves.

I had a connecting flight that I cannot make because your first leg was delayed by six hours. The rebooking you offered puts me into my destination twenty-six hours after the original arrival, with a layover in a city that is not even close to a direct route. The agent shrugged and said this is the best she could do. The best she could do is the worst itinerary I have seen in twenty years of flying. The airline as an institution is dead to me.

I would rather chew on a wet napkin than ever step foot in that pretentious little hellhole again. The host treated my reservation like a hostage negotiation, the chef apparently thinks salt is a war crime, and the bill came with a smug little note thanking me for supporting local cuisine. Local cuisine? Local extortion is more like it. The only thing authentic about that place is the contempt the staff has for paying customers.

Looping me in at the eleventh hour on a project that has been ongoing for six weeks, then demanding my input by end of day, is not collaboration. It is dumping. You did not plan, you did not communicate, and now you expect me to clean up the mess of your own poor management. I do not work for you. I work with you, and only because the org chart says so. Get your act together.

Form A says I need to submit Form B. Form B says I need to submit Form C. Form C says I need to first complete Form A. I am stuck in a paperwork loop that some sadistic civil servant designed forty years ago and no one has bothered to fix because the people who would fix it work in the same building that produced it. The whole system needs to be burned down and rebuilt from scratch.

Slow drivers in the left lane are a societal cancer. I do not care if you think you are doing the speed limit. I do not care if you believe you are morally superior. Move. Get over. The left lane is for passing, not for your meandering tour of the interstate at fifty-five miles an hour with a line of forty cars behind you. You are not a traffic-calming device. You are an obstruction. Move.

Stop telling me my opinion on contemporary art is wrong because I do not have an MFA. The art is being shown in a public museum, paid for in part by public funds, in a society where I am a member of the public. I am allowed to think it is terrible. The condescension from gallery staff when an ordinary person dares to express dislike is the exact reason this entire field is collapsing in on itself.

The water glasses have been empty since the moment we sat down. Refilling water is not a culinary achievement. It does not require training. It does not require a degree. It requires holding a pitcher and pointing it downward. And yet here we are, throats parched, watching the staff cluster near the door discussing weekend plans while paying customers slowly desiccate in booth seven.

The wedding venue tacked on a six-thousand-dollar service charge that was never mentioned in any contract or brochure and is, according to the contract, not gratuity, not tax, and not refundable. When pressed, the coordinator described it as standard. Standard is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence. Standard is the word used by people who know they cannot defend a charge on its merits and so they hide behind etiquette.

I asked to speak to a supervisor and was informed that no supervisor was available. None? Not one? In an entire call center of presumably hundreds of employees, no one in a position of authority happens to be on shift? The lie is so flimsy it would not survive contact with a curious child, and yet the company expects me to accept it. The contempt is breathtaking. The cynicism is corrosive.

The newsletter platform now charges to read your own back issues. Articles I wrote, hosted on their site, behind a paywall I am expected to pay them for. They have monetized the access to my own work. There is no word for this in polite company. The closest I can manage in print is an extortion racket dressed up as a software-as-a-service company, and I suspect the people running it know exactly what they are doing.

I asked for the bread basket twice. Twice. By the third request I had aged visibly. The bread, when it finally arrived, was a single roll, cold, accompanied by no butter. I asked for butter. The server said certainly and never returned. I ate the roll dry, in a state of seething acceptance, and resolved that this establishment had received the last dollar of my life it would ever see.

The autopay system charged me three times for the same monthly bill, and the refund is going to take eight to ten business days to process. Funny how the charges happened instantly and the refunds take a week and a half. Funny how every error in the billing always favors the company and never the customer. I am keeping records. I am submitting them to my state attorney general. And I am switching providers the moment a competitor enters this market.

The press release expresses regret. Regret. As if the executives had stepped on a colleague's toe at the elevator. Their decisions deprived families of their savings and they regret it the way you regret eating a second slice of cake. The disproportion between the harm caused and the tone of the apology is the actual insult, not the original wrongdoing, which by this point is almost beside the point.

The application crashed three times in the last hour, each time losing twenty minutes of unsaved work, and when I clicked submit on the bug report, the bug report itself crashed. The level of contempt this software has for its users is breathtaking. It is not even hiding it anymore. It is openly hostile, and I am paying a monthly subscription for the privilege of being abused.

I have submitted the same application four times. Each submission has been returned with a different reason for rejection. The first reason no longer applies. The second reason was the agency's own mistake. The third reason was a typo in their reply email. The fourth reason is illegible. I am beginning to suspect that no one is reading these applications and the rejection notices are being generated by a malfunctioning printer in a basement no one has visited since 1986.

The concert ticket has now arrived with a delivery fee of seven dollars, in addition to the original five-dollar service fee, and the new emerging-artist support fee, which the venue introduced last year without explaining what an emerging-artist support fee actually supports. The artist on the ticket is not emerging. The artist has been touring for twenty years. The fee is a sleight of hand and the fact that no one has sued over it is the eighth wonder of modern commerce.

Influencer culture has produced an entire generation of people who confuse attention with achievement. They have no skills, no expertise, no contributions to make to anything, and yet they are treated as authorities on health, finance, relationships, and politics. The platforms reward this. The audiences enable this. The whole arrangement is rotting the brain of the species and we are not even pretending to fight it anymore.

We have been sitting at this table for fifty-six minutes without so much as a glass of water. The waiter has walked past us nine times. He has made eye contact and looked away. Other tables that arrived after us are eating dessert. The hostess seated us, vanished, and has presumably gone home for the night. I am not asking for the moon. I am asking for menus, which were promised before the appetizer of indifference arrived.

The deductible is now equal to half a month's rent. The premium has tripled in five years. The coverage has narrowed to the point where the policy is essentially performative. We are paying for the right to be denied later. The pretense that this is insurance is a fraud. It is a tax with extra steps. And the executives running the show are making record profits while their customers ration medication and skip doctor visits to stay current on premiums.

The PDF form was downloaded, filled out, printed, signed, scanned, and uploaded back to the same site, where it was rejected because I did not use the latest version of the PDF, which is dated yesterday. The form was identical yesterday. The form is identical today. The version number has changed. The version number is the only thing that has changed. The institution has invented bureaucracy as performance art and I am the unpaid actor.

The detox is a lie. Your liver detoxes. Your kidneys detox. Your body has been detoxing for millions of years without any help from a stranger on Instagram selling you charcoal lemonade. The whole concept of a thirty-dollar juice cleansing your insides is pseudoscience dressed up in mason jars. Drink water. Eat vegetables. Stop falling for nonsense. The wellness industry has gaslit the public for a decade and we are still buying in.

Per my last email. Per my last email. Per my last email. I am sending this for the fourth time because apparently the previous three did not penetrate whatever cloud of obliviousness you operate within. The deadline was Tuesday. It is now Friday. I am cc-ing your manager because the polite escalation has clearly failed, and I am no longer willing to absorb the consequences of your refusal to do your job.

I missed my connection because the first flight was forty minutes late, after which they parked at a remote gate, after which the bus took twenty minutes to arrive, after which they unloaded the elderly first and the wheelchair passengers second and me, in seat 33F, last. By the time I reached the connecting gate it had closed five minutes earlier. The agent there laughed. Actually laughed. And told me to head to customer service to be rebooked, where the line is two hours long.

A pile of garbage on the floor of a museum is not art. It is a pile of garbage. The fact that the curator wrote a six-paragraph wall plaque about how it interrogates contemporary consumerism does not change what it is. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling you something, usually for six figures. The entire industry has become a money-laundering operation dressed up in academic prose, and the rest of us are expected to nod along.

They auto-renewed my annual subscription nine days before the renewal date, charged my card without notice, and then informed me that refunds are not issued on annual plans more than seventy-two hours after charging. The seventy-two hours had passed because I was not warned the charge was coming. It is a perfectly engineered trap and the company is proud of it. I can hear them being proud through the screen.

The traffic app told me this route would save twenty minutes. It did not save twenty minutes. It led me down a one-lane road behind a tractor going twelve miles an hour, then dumped me onto a closed street, then routed me back onto the original highway one exit before where I started. The algorithm is gaslighting me. The whole concept of helpful navigation is a lie. I would rather get lost using a paper map than be misled by another smug little app.

The hold music is doing psychological damage. It is the same eight seconds of off-brand smooth jazz looped without mercy, interrupted every twelve seconds by a voice telling me how much my call matters. If my call mattered I would not be the seventy-third caller in the queue. Stop lying. The whole thing is a calculated insult dressed up as customer service and I see it for what it is.

Your gate agent looked me dead in the eye and lied about the reason for the delay. There was no weather. The pilot was not late. The plane was not undergoing maintenance. I watched the crew stand around chatting for forty minutes while two hundred passengers boiled in a jetway. The audacity of being lied to in person, by an employee paid to lie, while paying for the privilege, is genuinely staggering. Train your people or fire them.

The agency lost my paperwork. They lost the original. They lost the copies I sent at their request. They have lost the documentation of having received the copies. They are now asking me to resubmit the entire packet for a third time, certified mail, at my expense, with no guarantee that this time it will be filed correctly. I am paying postage for the privilege of doing the agency's job for them.

There is a special circle of hell reserved for whoever decided that the optimal customer experience was eleven layers of menu, each one demanding a sixteen-digit account number that you cannot remember because you are trying to call about the bill that contains it. Every step is a trap. Every option leads back to the main menu. The hold music sounds like it was composed by a sociopath. I am losing years of my life to this telephonic labyrinth and somewhere an executive is collecting a bonus for inventing it.

There is a special place in my list of grievances for the people who stop in the middle of an active travel lane to let someone out of a parking spot. You are not chivalrous. You are not kind. You are causing a six-car pile-up behind you because you cannot understand the concept of waiting two seconds. Drive. Just drive. Get out of my way and stop making everyone else suffer for your imaginary politeness.

He scheduled a one-on-one to discuss why I missed a deadline. The deadline was missed because he asked for revisions to four different pieces of work the day before the deadline, none of which were urgent, all of which took the time I needed to finish the original task. He is now using the missed deadline as evidence that I struggle with time management. The audacity of the framing has rendered me speechless. I have prepared a written rebuttal. It will not change anything.

The exercise bike has a subscription. The water bottle has a subscription. The toothbrush has a subscription. The frying pan has a subscription, somehow, for access to the heat-mapping smart features that no human asked for. Everything in my house is now a node on a billing network and the only way to opt out is to throw the entire product in the trash and buy something dumb, which is, ironically, also getting harder to find.

The fact that we now have a thirty-million-dollar movie marketing budget for a film that did not even hire a writer worth fifty thousand dollars tells you everything about the priorities of this industry. They will spend more on a single billboard than on the script the entire enterprise rests on. Then they wonder why audiences are losing interest. They are losing interest because everything you make is the same hollow, calculated nothing.

The dentist office that charges thousands for procedures they later admit were unnecessary has now sued a former patient for posting a negative review. The negative review was true. The procedure was unnecessary. The lawsuit is a SLAPP designed to silence other patients. Well it is not going to work, because every single thing they do not want public is now public, and the local news has agreed to run the story next week.

That was the worst call I have ever seen in a professional game. Worst. Absolute worst. The replay was right there on the jumbotron, the entire stadium saw it, and the official looked at it for thirty seconds and somehow came out the other side with the wrong answer. Either the league is rigged or the officiating standard is so low that anyone with eyes should be embarrassed for them. Suspend him. Retrain him. Make him pay the fans for the ticket prices.

The fiber line in the alley has been hanging by a thread for two months because of a botched install your subcontractor performed on a neighbor's house. Every time a strong wind blows it knocks out the entire block. We have reported this. We have photographed it. We have sent video. Your company's response is to schedule another visit, which is always missed, and to send increasingly threatening notices about late payment for service that is barely intermittent.

The dropdown for billing address has me down as living in eleven different cities. The autocomplete has helpfully retained every typo, every old address, every state I have visited and once filled out a hotel form in. There is no way to clear the dropdown. There is no way to edit the list. The list grows every time I shop online. By the time I am eighty, the dropdown will contain my entire residential history and the names of cities I have never set foot in.

Roundabouts are not optional. They are not negotiable. They are not a fascinating cultural artifact for you to study from a complete stop in the middle of one. The yield sign means yield to traffic in the circle, not freeze in terror while a line of cars piles up behind you. Every roundabout in this town has become a humiliating monument to public stupidity, and I am genuinely starting to lose my mind.

Forty-three dollars for a hotel water bottle. Forty-three. The same brand sells for a dollar fifty at the gas station two blocks away. The hotel has not added gold leaf. It has not blessed the water. It has not flown it in from a glacier. It has merely placed it on a nightstand and slapped a fee on it that exceeds the cost of the room in some parts of the country. This is highway robbery with a turndown service.

A six-page letter about my mailbox. Six pages. About a mailbox. The HOA has decided that the slight deviation in the color of the post from the approved palette constitutes a violation of community standards and is fining me seventy-five dollars per week until I repaint it. Seventy-five dollars per week. For a color that is two shades off from a palette nobody can find a copy of. The pettiness is exhausting and the abuse of authority is unforgivable.

Four hundred pages of self-indulgent meandering, dressed up in the kind of prose that thinks it is profound when it is merely opaque. The narrator's inner monologue could have been condensed to a single chapter. The plot, such as it is, exists in the space between thoughts. By the time the protagonist finally has his epiphany at the end, I had stopped caring about him approximately three hundred pages earlier. A book to throw across the room.

He has asked me to forward him every email I receive from any client before I respond, so he can approve the response. The volume of emails makes this impossible. He acknowledges this. He has not changed the policy. He simply expects compliance with an unworkable rule and gets quietly furious when responses go out without his blessing. He is angry about the very thing he made impossible. The contradiction is the management style.

Hand to the face is no longer a penalty unless the referee feels like making it one. Holding is no longer a penalty unless the referee feels like making it one. Pass interference is whatever the referee says it is on any given Sunday. The inconsistency is killing the sport. Make the rules clear, enforce them uniformly, and stop ruining games with arbitrary judgment calls that no one can predict from one drive to the next.

Auto-correct just changed my colleague's name to something obscene for the fourth time today, and the option to add custom words is buried so deep in the settings I would need a sherpa to find it. The keyboard you ship with this device is actively undermining my professional life. Every email I send is a roll of the dice. I would rather type on a typewriter from 1962 than continue to fight this digital saboteur masquerading as a productivity tool.

I have called six times this week and each time I am told a credit will be applied to my next bill. The next bill arrived yesterday with no credit. I called again. They told me to wait for the credit, which is being processed. Processed by whom? By what? It has been processed for nine business days and the only thing being processed is my patience, which is now thoroughly minced.

Every app I downloaded last year is now demanding a subscription to access features that were free at launch. The flashlight wants three dollars a month. The notes app wants five. The weather app wants seven. The weather is the same weather everyone else has for free. The flashlight is a flashlight. I refuse to pay rent to access functionality that existed in a 2009 phone for no money at all.

The upstairs neighbor stomps. Constantly. Heel-first. Across hardwood floors. At eleven at night. At three in the morning. At five-thirty when she leaves for work. I have asked her to be considerate. I have asked the landlord to intervene. I have considered installing a mirror on the ceiling so I can stare upward at the source of my torment. The landlord shrugs. The neighbor shrugs. The shrugs accumulate into a posture of institutional indifference.

Subscription software is a moral failure. I do not want to rent my word processor for the rest of my life. I want to buy it, own it, and use it without you reaching back into my wallet every thirty days. The fact that I can no longer open files I created with my own labor without paying you monthly tribute is theft dressed up as innovation, and I resent every single one of you who normalized this nightmare.

The presenter just spent eleven minutes explaining the agenda before starting on item one. Eleven minutes. To explain what is written on the screen behind him in twelve-point font. The agenda is not the meeting. The agenda is the preamble to the meeting. Why are we spending a fifth of our allotted time discussing the discussion we are about to have. This is meta-procrastination dressed up as professionalism.

I am not going through your stupid five-minute video for the answer to a question that could have been a sentence. The whole platform has trained creators to pad their content into bloated multi-minute episodes because the algorithm rewards watch time over usefulness. The result is endless yapping with the actual information buried at minute four-twelve, if it appears at all. I have lost so many hours to this nonsense.

If you forward me one more LinkedIn article about emotional intelligence in the workplace I am going to lose what little composure I have left. The irony of you, of all people, lecturing the team about empathy and active listening is so thick I could choke on it. Practice what you preach. Or better yet, stop preaching, because nobody asked, nobody is impressed, and we all see exactly who you are.

Calling that a burger is an insult to ground beef everywhere. It was a hockey puck on a soggy bun with a wilted leaf of something pretending to be lettuce. The fries were limp and salt-starved. The milkshake tasted like chalk. And the server had the nerve to ask if I wanted dessert, as if I would willingly submit to another round of culinary punishment from this overpriced cafeteria.

Stop remaking every film from the eighties. We have seen them. They were fine the first time. Your reboot adds nothing except a coat of digital paint and the smug self-awareness of a screenwriter who thinks meta commentary is a substitute for an original idea. There are thousands of writers with original scripts in drawers. Read one of them. Hire one of them. Stop strip-mining nostalgia for a quick paycheck.

The advance fee scam keeps working because the scammers cast such a wide net that even a one percent response rate generates enormous profit. Every single person reading this knows about Nigerian princes. Everyone knows the lawyer holding millions for a long-lost relative is fake. And yet the emails keep coming, because somewhere out there, someone is still falling for it. I do not blame the victims. I blame the regulators who could shut this down and choose not to.

I worked at this company for three years and I am posting this on my way out the door because I cannot in good conscience let another candidate walk into that place blind. The pay is below market. The benefits are deceptive. The manager screams at people in front of clients. The HR department exists to protect the company from the employees. Do not apply. Do not interview. And if you are already there, get out while you still have your sanity.

I denied the location permission and the app has stopped functioning. The app does not require location for any of its features. The app does require location for its business model, which is selling my location to data brokers. The app has held its functionality hostage to my permission grant. The choice is now between using the app and giving up information that has no business being part of this transaction. I will uninstall the app. I will leave a one-star review. I will recommend that others do the same.

When you took credit for the report I wrote during yesterday's meeting, in front of the entire leadership team, you crossed a line that I cannot pretend did not happen. I drafted every paragraph. I built every chart. You did not even read the document before you walked into that room and called it our work. We are not a we. Do not ever do that again. I am keeping receipts now.

The update reset all my preferences. My carefully curated settings, accumulated over years of refinement, are gone. The dark mode has reverted to light mode. The notifications have re-enabled themselves. The default zoom level is wrong. The keyboard shortcuts have been remapped. Every single bit of personalization I had configured is gone, and the developers consider this an acceptable side effect of progress. I do not.

I was charged seventy dollars to check a bag that weighed exactly the same as the carry-on I was forced to gate-check for free because your overhead bins are designed for handbags and pity. Your business model is built on lying about prices and then ambushing customers at the counter with fees they had no way to anticipate. It is dishonest. It is predatory. It is the kind of behavior that makes me actively root for your bankruptcy.

The robotic woman on the menu has the gall to ask if I am satisfied with my service before I have spoken to a single human being. Satisfied. I have been ricocheting through this menu like a pinball for two hours, the system has hung up on me twice, and the only living creature involved in this transaction so far is the fly buzzing around my kitchen. No, I am not satisfied. I have never been less satisfied in my entire life.

Performance art has become an excuse for self-indulgent narcissism with no technical skill required. The artist sits in a chair and stares at people. That is the piece. That is the entire piece. The line of fawning critics wrapped around the block to experience this profound encounter. There was no encounter. There was a person sitting in a chair, and a great many fools convinced themselves it was meaningful so they would not feel left out of the discourse.

Their apology started with the phrase we hear you, which is the universal corporate signal that they did not hear me, are not going to hear me, and would prefer that I stop making noise so the news cycle moves on. The substance of the apology consisted entirely of vague promises to listen better and to engage in ongoing dialogue. There were no specifics. There were no resignations. There was no money. There was no action. There was only the carefully measured cadence of contrition delivered by people who have done this many times before and will do it many times again.

The pharmacy raised the price of my prescription by four hundred percent overnight with no warning. Same pill. Same dose. Same factory. Four times the price. When I asked why I was told it was a manufacturer change, which is corporate speak for we found out we could and so we did. People need this medication to function. The fact that there is a market mechanism that allows this is a moral failure of the species.

The marketing called this book a literary masterpiece. The marketing lied. The book is a baggy, pretentious, overwritten exercise in writerly vanity. Every chapter contains at least one sentence so purple it should be reported to color authorities. The metaphors come in herds. The adjectives are stacked like cordwood. Whoever edited this manuscript was either too intimidated or too lazy to do their job. The reader pays the price.

The smell coming off you from across the room is genuinely toxic. There is a shower. There is deodorant. There are basic standards of hygiene that should not need to be enforced by management. The other patrons should not have to hold their breath when you walk past. The whole concept of a shared space relies on shared courtesy, and you are bringing the average way down. Bathe. Please. For all of us.

The CAPTCHA has asked me to identify crosswalks fourteen times. I have identified them fourteen times. It does not believe me. I am clearly a human. I am clearly the kind of human who is increasingly furious with the platform that demands I prove my humanity at every turn. The robot detector is broken. The site has decided that I am suspicious. The site will not let me complete the task I came here to do. The site has won, by attrition, and I have lost, by being a person.

The phone bill includes a fee for paper billing, a fee for not enrolling in autopay, a regulatory cost recovery fee that is not a tax but resembles one, a federal universal service fee, an administrative fee that is described nowhere in the contract, and a 911 emergency services fee that the carrier appears to keep rather than remit. None of these fees were disclosed when I signed up. All of these fees are non-negotiable.

I posted a photo of my new garden and three strangers in the comments have informed me that the soil is the wrong pH, that the spacing is incorrect, that the plant choices are unsustainable, and that I should consider native species, the wisdom of permaculture, and a particular YouTube channel that will, they assure me, change my life. I did not ask for the YouTube channel. I do not want the lecture. I am happy with the garden. The internet has decided otherwise.

Merging is not a competitive sport. It is not a contest of wills. It is not a metaphor for your tortured masculinity. It is two lanes becoming one, a process so simple that every other species on earth could probably manage it, and yet here we are, watching grown adults play chicken at the on-ramp like absolute fools. The next person who refuses to let me merge gets nothing but pure, distilled contempt.

Your dog barks for six hours straight every single day while you are at work, and the fact that you cannot hear it does not mean it is not happening. The rest of the cul-de-sac can hear it. The mailman can hear it. The poor animal is clearly miserable, you are clearly negligent, and I am out of patience. Get a trainer. Get a sitter. Get rid of the dog. But stop pretending this is fine when it is so obviously, audibly not.

Reversing a clean catch six minutes after the play because some bored producer in a video booth thought he saw a wobble is not officiating, it is theater. The rule was clear. The catch was complete. The runner was already on the bench. Inventing a replay reversal to swing the game in the final minutes is the kind of thing that erodes public trust in the entire league, and the commissioner should be losing sleep over it. Apparently he is not.

The search function in this app is genuinely worse than scrolling through every folder by hand. It cannot find files I just saved. It returns results from accounts I closed years ago. It ignores the exact phrase I typed in quotes. I have spent more time fighting your search than I would have spent organizing my files manually, and the whole point of using a computer was to avoid that. You have failed at the one thing you needed to do.

Your handyman shows up two hours late, does the job badly, leaves a mess, and you charge me for the inconvenience. That is not a service. That is a hostage situation in a workshop apron. I would rather fix things myself than continue to invite this person into my home to make problems worse and then bill me for the privilege. Find a new handyman or learn to use a wrench yourself.

Predictive text just suggested I conclude my work email with kind regrets instead of kind regards. The suggestion is technically grammatical. The suggestion is unhinged. The suggestion came after I had typed kind reg, which is unambiguously the beginning of regards in the context of an email signature. The autocomplete is editorializing. The autocomplete has opinions about my professional relationships. The autocomplete needs to be taken outside and disabled.

The car alarm has been going off for forty minutes. The owner is nowhere to be found. The alarm is doing its job, which is to be unbearable, and is failing its job, which is to summon the owner. The car will continue alarming until someone breaks a window in frustration. The neighborhood is not concerned about the car. The neighborhood is concerned about whoever loses control first and the litigation that may follow.

We have multiple new reports from current employees, all corroborating that the culture has not changed and the executives accused of misconduct are still in place. The apology was a lie. The reforms were a lie. The company is exactly what it was, just with better media training.
